---
title: "Centering a predictor"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The intercept of a regression is the fitted conditional mean where every predictor equals zero. **Centering** changes that reference value while preserving all fitted comparisons.

Here the response remains the [Provo word position mean](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) among readers with a retained positive first fixation. Moving the surprisal origin neither restores skipped reader by word trials nor changes the passage grouping.

The sample [standard deviation](../random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd) later supplies one possible scaling constant. We provisionally call $y_i-\widehat y_i$ a **residual**, the observed value minus the fitted value. We derive its regression properties when we turn to [residuals](residuals.qmd).

What must remain unchanged when the predictor origin moves? The Provo algebra below answers by tracking the intercept, slope, fitted values, and residuals under the reparameterization.

Suppose we shift the predictor origin by a constant $c$ and define $x^c=x-c$. The observation at $x=c$ now has $x^c=0$. Rewriting the same line changes the intercept because zero names a different predictor value, while preserving the slope and every fitted value. We will verify each claim with the observed Provo fit below.

## Reparameterizing the Provo regression

Let $X_i$ be [modeled cloze
surprisal](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data), the negative base 2
logarithm of the fitted cloze probability, and let $c$ be its observed sample
mean. Define

$$
X_i^c=X_i-c.
$$

The notation distinguishes four objects. $X_i$ is a random predictor before sampling; $x_i$ is its observed value; $\overline x$ is the [estimator](../statistical-inference/properties-of-estimators.qmd) that computes a sample mean; and $c=\overline x(\mathbf x)$ is the realized constant used to construct $x_i^c=x_i-c$. It is not asserted to be a known population mean.

Notice what we have and have not done. We have subtracted one constant from every observed predictor value. We have not divided by a scale. The latter operation is usually called **standardizing** when the scale is a standard deviation; it changes the size of one predictor unit and hence changes the numerical slope. Centering alone changes where zero falls.

The uncentered line can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
m(X_i)
&=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i\\
&=\beta_0+\beta_1(X_i^c+c)\\
&=(\beta_0+\beta_1c)+\beta_1X_i^c.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus centering changes the intercept from $\beta_0$ to $\beta_0+\beta_1c$. It leaves the slope and every fitted value unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: center-provo-surprisal
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
surprisal_center <- mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - surprisal_center

fit_uncentered <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)
fit_centered <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c,
  data = provo
)

maximum_fit_difference <- max(abs(
  fitted(fit_uncentered) - fitted(fit_centered)
))
slope_difference <- unname(
  coef(fit_uncentered)[["cloze_surprisal_bits"]] -
    coef(fit_centered)[["cloze_surprisal_c"]]
)

stopifnot(
  maximum_fit_difference < 1e-12,
  abs(slope_difference) < 1e-12
)

rbind(
  uncentered = coef(fit_uncentered),
  centered = coef(fit_centered)
)
```

The first row lets us check the code against the algebra directly:

```{r}
#| label: show-one-centered-provo-row
data.frame(
  original_surprisal = provo$cloze_surprisal_bits[[1L]],
  center = surprisal_center,
  centered_surprisal = provo$cloze_surprisal_c[[1L]],
  checked_difference =
    provo$cloze_surprisal_bits[[1L]] - surprisal_center
)
```

The observed center is `r sprintf("%.3f", surprisal_center)` bits. After centering, the intercept is `r sprintf("%.4f", coef(fit_centered)[["(Intercept)"]])`, the fitted mean at that observed predictor average. The two slopes differ by only `r format(abs(slope_difference), scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`, and the largest difference between fitted values is `r format(maximum_fit_difference, scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-centered-line
#| fig-cap: "The Provo regression on the centered predictor scale. The vertical reference marks observed mean modeled cloze surprisal."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_c = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_c),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_c),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$fitted <- predict(fit_centered, newdata = grid)

point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_c, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(cloze_surprisal_c, fitted),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal minus its observed mean (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

Centering does not make the slope more causal, remove passage dependence, remove collinearity, or “control” a variable. It changes the coordinate system used to describe the same fitted line.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which original surprisal value receives centered value zero?
2. Why is the centered intercept more directly supported by the observations?
3. Which fitted quantities must remain invariant under centering?
4. Would dividing by a standard deviation still be centering alone?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The observed sample mean of modeled cloze surprisal receives centered value zero. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The centered intercept represents the fitted response at the observed mean surprisal, rather than at zero surprisal, which may be poorly supported by the data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The slope, every fitted value, every residual, and predictions expressed at the same original predictor values must remain unchanged. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. No. Dividing by a standard deviation also rescales the predictor and changes the coefficient's unit. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

We next change the [response scale](response-transformations.qmd) rather than the predictor reference.
